conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Claire, a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. Today I’ll be using a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling during the past seven days. It’s simply a way for us to check in on your emotional well-being, not a test you can “pass” or “fail.” Everything you share stays between us unless you or your baby’s safety is at risk. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions; I’ll re-phrase each one in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, has it felt easy and natural, or has it felt forced and difficult?

Honestly, it’s been hard. My best friend came over the other day and told a silly story that normally would have had me in stitches, but I had to fake a little chuckle. Nothing feels truly funny right now—I’m too tired and worried most of the time.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really. Most of the time I feel like I’m just going through the motions, so even when something should be funny, it doesn’t reach me. I’ll try to smile so people don’t worry, but inside I just feel flat or on-edge about the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much lately. I used to get excited about little things—grabbing coffee with a friend, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just ticking off the hours. Sometimes I plan something small, like watching a show while I pump, but when the time comes I’m too tired or anxious to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... a lot of the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it's something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not holding her right, or I'm just not cut out for this. Last night she wouldn't settle after a feeding and I sat there crying, convinced it was because I'm a "bad mom." Rationally I know babies cry, but the guilt still crashes over me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. Even when she’s sleeping soundly, I’ll suddenly feel my heart race and check the monitor five times in ten minutes, worried she’s stopped breathing. If she spits up a little more than usual, I’m googling reflux or allergies. I know most of it’s normal baby stuff, but I can’t turn the worry off—it just keeps looping in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—like yesterday, I was folding her onesies and suddenly felt this rush of dread, my chest went tight and I couldn’t catch my breath. It lasted a few minutes and then faded, but it’s scary when it happens. There’s no real reason; it just feels like my body’s stuck on high-alert.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days. Between feedings, diaper changes, and trying to grab a little sleep, I feel like I’m drowning. Some mornings I open my eyes and already feel behind. I keep lists in my head—laundry, bottles, pumping, texts I haven’t answered—and it all piles up until I’m just frozen on the couch watching her sleep, too overwhelmed to move.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get her down, crawl into bed myself, but my mind won’t shut off—running through everything I might’ve done wrong or imagining worst-case scenarios. I’ll lie there for an hour or more, drifting in and out, then jolt awake at every little sound she makes. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. There are moments when I look at her and feel this wave of love, but it’s quickly followed by this heavy, gray sadness I can’t shake. I’ll just sit there with tears sliding down, feeling empty even while I’m holding her. It’s like the joy is trapped behind a thick wall and all I can reach is the ache.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been a few times this week. Sometimes it’s because I’m exhausted, sometimes it’s just this sudden wave of sadness that hits while I’m rocking her. Last night I burst into tears when my partner asked how my day was—nothing bad had even happened, I just felt overwhelmed and couldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve felt really low, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and gray-how even moments that once brought smiles now leave you flat or quietly on-edge, and how waves of guilt and worry crash over you many times a day. Your descriptions of feeling "drowning" in daily tasks, lying awake with racing thoughts, and crying easily show how hard you're working to care for your baby while carrying a deep, persistent sadness.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete inability to experience humor or joy, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly reports diminished enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure, mapping to "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a lot of the time" with vivid examples of feeling responsible for baby's crying and labeling herself a "bad mom," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, hard-to-control worry about baby's breathing, reflux, etc., matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic-like episodes with physical symptoms and no clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, feeling "drowning" and "frozen"—clear inability to cope.</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences sleep difficulty most nights this week, lying awake over an hour with racing thoughts and fragmented sleep, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, overwhelming sadness that intrudes even during moments of love for her baby, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by exhaustion and sudden sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 24 far exceeds the 12+ threshold indicating high probability of major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed the most severe option on items measuring low mood, loss of enjoyment, self-blame, and anxiety, plus frequent crying and impaired sleep. These align with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood, diminished interest, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and concentration difficulty nearly every day for two weeks. The intensity of <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> and constant worry about your baby also suggests comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</mod>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent evaluation with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>maternal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and discuss risks and benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist partner or family to handle a set of night duties so you can obtain four to five hours of uninterrupted sleep; practice wind-down routines like dim lights and no screens after feeds
4. Schedule brief daily "you-time" (10-15 min) for a walk, shower, or music while a trusted adult watches the baby
5. Reach out to local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or online communities to reduce isolation and share experiences
6. Keep the national <med>Maternal Mental Health Hotline</med> number accessible for 24/7 emotional support
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS in two weeks with your provider to monitor symptom change and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire

Areas of clinical significance  
1. Depressive symptoms  
   – Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
   – Excessive self-blame / guilt (“bad mom” cognitions) (Q3)  
   – Sleep disturbance triggered by ruminative worry (Q7)  

2. Anxiety symptoms  
   – Near-daily uncontrolled worry about infant safety (Q4)  
   – Episodic panic-type sensations without clear trigger (tight chest, breathlessness) (Q5)  
   – Subjective “high-alert” state (Q4, Q5)  

3. Functional impact  
   – Overwhelm, task paralysis, sense of “drowning” (Q6)  
   – Loss of anticipatory pleasure for previously enjoyed activities (Q2)  

Protective / safety factors  
– Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)  
– Endorses love for infant and motivation “to feel better” for baby

Risk profile  
High likelihood of major depressive and anxiety symptoms in postpartum period; meets threshold for further clinical evaluation (e.g., EPDS ≥12, GAD-7 likely moderate-high) and possible referral to maternal mental health specialty services.

Next steps (for provider)  
– Complete EPDS or PHQ-9/GAD-7 for quantification  
– Assess social supports, partner involvement, history of mood disorders  
– Provide psycho-education, safety planning, and linkage to evidence-based treatment resources
